title: The promise kept
hookLine: the oldest telling of the young wanderer and King Bimbisara, and what happened years later

lines: DAY 41: A KING ON A TERRACE.
cards: On day forty-one, a young wanderer walked through Rajagaha with his bowl, and a king on a palace terrace couldn't stop watching him. The king offered him an army and a fortune. The young man said no.
That was more than a year and a half ago on this path. Now the Sutta Nipata's Great Chapter opens with that same scene, in what may be one of the oldest tellings of it. First, its own plain words.
Then the story, forward, to what happened when the wanderer came back.

teach.h: EYES LOWERED, A PLOW'S LENGTH AHEAD
teach.b: The poem is the Pabbajja Sutta, the going forth, and tradition says Ananda speaks it. King Bimbisara sees a young man walking for alms, eyes lowered, looking only a plow's length ahead.
His messengers find him eating on a hillside outside the city. The king drives out, steps down from his chariot, and makes the offer: you're young and noble-looking; lead my army, take wealth.
The young man answers simply. My people live beside the Himalaya, among the Kosalans, rich and energetic, Sakyans by birth.

teach.h: I DIDN'T LEAVE HOME FOR PLEASURES
teach.b: I didn't leave home to find pleasures. I've seen the danger in them, and the safety in letting go. I'm going to strive; that's where my heart is glad.
And the poem ends there. In this old poem, there's no promise to return.

teach.h: THE PROMISE COMES IN LATER TELLINGS
teach.b: That comes in later tellings: the king asks, if you find what you seek, come back and teach me first, and he agrees. The monastic texts tell how it was kept. After awakening, the Buddha walked back to Rajagaha.
The king came out with a great crowd to hear him, and understood.
Then Bimbisara said that as a young prince he'd had five wishes: to be crowned, that an awakened one would come to his kingdom, that he could honor him, that he'd be taught, and that he'd understand.
All five, he said, have come true today. He gave the community a park, the Bamboo Grove, and the Buddha accepted it.
A promise made on a hillside, kept years later.

how: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara's gift of the Bamboo Grove to the community, and pilgrims to Rajgir in India visit both the Bamboo Grove and the hills where the young wanderer is said to have met the king.

coming home after years of searching

games.q: you're the young wanderer. the king offers you an army and a fortune. how do you answer, in the old poem?
o: accept, and use it to do good.
tell him who you are and that you're going to strive.
games.why: he names his people and birth, says he saw the danger in pleasures and the safety in letting go, and says he's going to strive.

practice: Picture the hillside: a young man with a bowl, a king stepping down from his chariot, two people who would meet again. Think of a promise someone kept to you, maybe years later than you expected, and if gratitude comes, let it.
Then hold one promise of your own not yet kept, gently, without scolding yourself, and see the first step back toward it.

wordCard.voice: Pabbajja, going forth. The young wanderer refuses a king's fortune, and in later tellings promises to return; awakened, he comes back, and all five of the king's wishes come true.

orig.note: Pali pabbajja: going forth, leaving home for the homeless life. the name of Sn 3.1.

carryVoice: Your line: take the first step. A promise can wait years and still be kept. Six hundred days on the path.
